subject: Communication
title: Positions vs. Interests
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Positions vs. Interests.

hook.text: Two sisters fight over the last orange. They cut it in half. One eats the fruit, the other uses the peel for baking.

buildup.text: Their positions were identical (I want the orange), but their interests were different (fruit vs. peel).

discovery.text: Fisher and Ury's 'Getting to Yes' taught: always negotiate interests, not positions.

twist.text: Interests are why they want it. Two people demanding the same office might want sunlight vs. quiet — both achievable.

climax.text: Most conflicts dissolve when you stop arguing about what and start asking why.

punchline.text: Don't fight over the orange. Ask why they want it.

quiz.question: What book introduced the positions vs. interests framework?

details.summary: Positions are stated demands; interests are the underlying needs driving those demands. Two people fighting over an orange may both want it (position), but one needs the juice and the other needs the peel. Uncovering interests opens creative solutions invisible at the position level.
details.whyItMatters: Most conflicts stall at the position level. The moment you shift to interests, solutions multiply dramatically.
takeaways: Positions are what people say they want
Interests are why they want it

faq.question: How do you uncover someone's underlying interests?
faq.answer: Ask 'why' and 'what would that give you' repeatedly. Listen for emotional cues that signal deeper needs like respect, security, or autonomy. Often people have not articulated their interests even to themselves, so patient questioning helps both sides discover them.

faq.question: Where does the positions versus interests concept come from?
faq.answer: Roger Fisher and William Ury popularized it in their 1981 book Getting to Yes. The orange example is their most famous illustration. The concept has become a cornerstone of negotiation training in business, law, and diplomacy worldwide.
